output.summary: SE management in idiopathic generalized epilepsy: benzodiazepine as first-line; IV valproate preferred for JME over phenytoin, which may worsen myoclonic components. Rhabdomyolysis complicating SE: aggressive IV hydration targeting urine output 1–2 mL/kg/h. Evidence supports medication adherence and trigger avoidance (sleep deprivation, alcohol) as primary SE prevention strategies in JME.

output.summary: Rhabdomyolysis from seizures: CK elevation above 5000 U/L is associated with higher acute kidney injury risk. patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Allen is a 32-year-old man with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy on valproic acid who is brought by ambulance after his roommates found him in a generalized tonic-clonic seizure that did not stop. The seizure began approximately 20 minutes prior to EMS arrival. He had been awake and appeared his normal self earlier that morning. His roommates are not aware of whether he took his medication last night or this morning. He had worked a late shift at the bar last night and drank significant alcohol afterward. He appears to have had only 3-4 hours of sleep. He has no known prior episodes of status epilepticus. His JME was diagnosed at age 17 and has been incompletely controlled on valproate due to inconsistent medication adherence. He has had several breakthrough seizures over the years, typically associated with sleep deprivation and alcohol use, which are well-known triggers for JME. On EMS arrival he was in continuous generalized tonic-clonic activity. Paramedics administered diazepam 10 mg IV en route without termination of seizures. He arrives to the ED in active status epilepticus, still convulsing.
